analysis.one_liner: Requires automakers to sell only zero-emission passenger cars by 2035.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, sent to a subcommittee a week later, and sat there until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The ZEVs Act would amend the Clean Air Act to set a national zero-emission vehicle standard. Starting in model year 2027, automakers would have to deliver a rising share of zero-emission cars each year — 43% in 2027, climbing to 100% by 2035 — verified through a government-issued credit system. Automakers that fall short would have to buy credits from competitors or pay a civil penalty equal to twice the value of the missing credits, and after 2035 the EPA could block manufacture of any new gasoline-powered passenger vehicle.
analysis.who_benefits: People living with tailpipe pollution gain cleaner air — the bill's own findings cite thousands of premature deaths and millions of serious illnesses each year from vehicle soot and smog, and transportation as the largest source of U.S. greenhouse gas emissions [S3]. Communities near highways and ports bear a disproportionate share of that pollution. Automakers that already lead on electric vehicles (such as Tesla and other EV-focused manufacturers) gain a new revenue stream, since they can sell their excess zero-emission credits to competitors that fall behind [S3]. State governments keep their power to set stricter rules, since the bill explicitly preserves California-style state programs [S3]. Drivers would eventually get an all-electric new-car market with lower fuel and maintenance costs, though the transition period could mean higher sticker prices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities exposed to tailpipe pollution; leading EV makers

how_it_helps.text: Sets a binding schedule requiring manufacturers to deliver 43% zero-emission vehicles by model year 2027, rising annually to 100% by 2035, after which only zero-emission passenger vehicles could be sold.

The bill's findings state that vehicle soot and smog cause thousands of premature deaths and millions of serious illnesses every year, and that transportation is the largest source of U.S. greenhouse gas emissions — pollution this mandate would phase out.

Creates an enforceable system: manufacturers that miss their quota must submit credits or pay a civil penalty worth twice the value of the shortfall, with penalties deposited into the Highway Trust Fund.
Preserves the authority of states to adopt stricter zero-emission vehicle requirements, so states like California could move faster than the federal floor.

analysis.who_pays: Conventional automakers and their suppliers bear the main cost: retooling product lines to meet rising zero-emission quotas and, if they fall short, paying penalties worth double the value of the missing credits [S3]. Those costs, and the price of credits bought from competitors, would likely be passed into new-vehicle prices, so new-car buyers would feel some of the burden during the transition. The oil industry loses a shrinking market for gasoline. The bill directs the EPA to run the credit and enforcement program but provides no dedicated funding in the text for charging infrastructure, leaving that gap to other laws.
analysis.who_pays_short: Conventional automakers, their suppliers, and oil producers

drawbacks.text: The credit-trading system lets manufacturers that lead on electric vehicles profit from competitors' shortfalls, and the bill explicitly authorizes a national credit market — a cost that lagging automakers would likely recover through higher prices on the gasoline cars they keep selling during the transition.

The civil penalty is set at twice the value of the missing credits, a stiff cost that would either push prices up or be absorbed by manufacturers; the bill offers no direct consumer subsidy or affordability provision, only a non-binding 'sense of Congress' that manufacturers should diversify models to protect consumer choice.

Starting at 43% in model year 2027 is aggressive relative to where the market stood when the bill was introduced, and the text contains no flexibility valve (such as hardship relief) if charging infrastructure or supply chains lag, raising the risk of compliance costs rather than sales.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health and climate gains are large and permanent — eliminating tailpipe emissions from new cars — while the costs fall on a concentrated industry and, partially, on new-car buyers during a roughly decade-long transition. The design is defensible but not generous to consumers: it leans on industry penalties and credit trading rather than direct help for buyers, and it funds no charging buildout itself. An honest supporter would acknowledge that the 2027 start and the doubling of penalties give manufacturers strong incentives to raise prices rather than miss quotas.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, sent to a subcommittee on March 8, 2024, and no further action was ever taken before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Levin introduced the Zero-Emission Vehicles Act of 2024 on February 29, 2024, with seven original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On March 8, 2024, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Environment, Manufacturing, and Critical Materials — the last action of any kind recorded.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Conventional automakers and oil producers are better off, since no zero-emission sales mandate, credit obligation, or penalty was ever enacted, and the status quo of voluntary EV targets and existing emissions rules continued.

for.name: Rep. Mike Levin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded its referral to Energy and Commerce.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, sent the bill to the Subcommittee on Environment, Manufacturing, and Critical Materials, and never scheduled a markup or vote; the bill saw no action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the only record signal is that all nine sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, while the Republican-led committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would force a rapid shift of their product lines to zero-emission vehicles, with penalties worth double the value of any credit shortfall if they miss quotas — costs they would likely pass to buyers. Many already sell EVs and could earn credits, but their core gasoline business would be on a path to a 2035 endpoint.

A 2035 endpoint on new gasoline passenger vehicles would shrink the market for motor fuel over time. The industry's interest in keeping gasoline car sales running indefinitely runs against the air-quality and climate benefits the bill targets.

The credit system turns every zero-emission vehicle sold into a tradeable asset, locking in EV makers as the gatekeepers of other manufacturers' compliance and giving leaders like Tesla a revenue stream from selling credits. Their interest in the bill runs alongside the public's cleaner-air interest, though credit prices flow into car costs.

Dealers are excluded from the definition of regulated vehicle manufacturers, so they face no direct mandate, but their inventory would have to convert to electric models and the bill preserves state-level rules they often contest.
